race=None: fixed:      copy 32 bytes into 64-byte buffer
race=4096: vulnerable: copy 4096 bytes into 64-byte buffer  OUT OF BOUNDS
race=4096: fixed:      copy 32 bytes into 64-byte buffer

blocks.md:
**History repeats: Cloudburst, 2009.** Sixteen years earlier, VMware's VMSA-2009-0006 fixed CVE-2009-1244, "a critical vulnerability in the virtual machine display function" that "might allow a guest operating system to run code on the host". Kostya Kortchinsky of Immunity presented it at Black Hat USA 2009 as **Cloudburst**: "3/4 bugs" in the emulated SVGA II video card, such as a 2D copy command whose signed bounds checks let a guest read and write host memory, in Workstation, Fusion and ESX alike.

**Trend data: Pwn2Own.** VMware products have been targets in Pwn2Own, the hacking contest run by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), since 2016. At Pwn2Own Berlin on 16 May 2025, Nguyen Hoang Thach of STAR Labs SG "used a single integer overflow to exploit VMware ESXi - a first in Pwn2Own history", earning USD 150,000; the next day Corentin Bayet of REverse Tactics exploited ESXi with two bugs and Synacktiv's team exploited Workstation. Broadcom's VMSA-2025-0013 (July 2025) fixed the bugs: in VMXNET3, VMCI, PVSCSI and vSockets, all virtual devices.

Escapes are chains: a device bug for code execution in the per-VM process, often a leak to make it reliable, then a sandbox or kernel bug to reach the host. Each link is a place to defend: fewer devices, a tight per-VM sandbox, and fast patching when a vendor says "exploited in the wild".

blocks.question: In VMSA-2025-0004, why was CVE-2025-22225 (kernel write) needed if CVE-2025-22224 already gave code execution?
options: It was not needed; the two are alternatives
22225 was needed to log in to the guest first
22224 gives code execution only as the per-VM VMX process, which is sandboxed; 22225 lets code in that process write the kernel and escape the sandbox
22225 bypasses the IOMMU
blocks.explain: Broadcom's own text: 22224 yields execution 'as the virtual machine's VMX process', and 22225 lets an actor 'with privileges within the VMX process' trigger a kernel write 'leading to an escape of the sandbox'. The sandbox forced a chain.

blocks.question: In the double-fetch toy, which change fixes the bug?
options: Reading the length from shared memory once into host memory, then checking and using that copy
Checking the length twice
Adding a sleep between the reads
Making BUF_LEN larger
blocks.explain: The guest can change shared memory at any time. Only a private copy is stable between check and use. Checking twice still leaves a window; a sleep widens it; a bigger buffer just moves the limit.

lessons.title: Case: Hyper-V's vmswitch, and how to read a hypervisor advisory

blocks.md: **Recall the design** from lesson 5: a Hyper-V guest's synthetic network card is a VSC (virtualization service consumer) in the guest that sends requests over VMBus to a VSP (virtualization service provider) in the root partition. For networking, that VSP is the host driver `vmswitch.sys`, the virtual switch. It is kernel code in the partition that controls the hardware, reachable by messages every guest can send. (The Windows kernel and driver security course, *Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening*, covers how Windows itself also uses Hyper-V for virtualization-based security, VBS.)

**CVE-2021-28476** was fixed on 11 May 2021 and scored 9.9 by Microsoft. MSRC's FAQ explains the impact: "This issue allows a guest VM to force the Hyper-V host's kernel to read from an arbitrary, potentially invalid address." Usually that means a host **bugcheck** (a blue-screen crash), taking down every VM on it. But "it is possible to read from a memory mapped device register corresponding to a hardware device attached to the Hyper-V host which may trigger additional, hardware device specific side effects that could compromise the Hyper-V host's security."

blocks.title: The vmswitch path (simplified from the finders' write-up)

scenes.caption: The guest's network driver sends an RNDIS (Remote Network Driver Interface Specification) message carrying an OID (object identifier) request: a query or setting for the virtual NIC.
VMBus delivers it to the networking VSP in the root partition's kernel.
One OID wraps an inner request that holds a pointer. vmswitch used that guest-supplied value without validating it.
The host kernel reads from the address the guest chose: usually a crash of the whole host; if it hits a device register, device-specific side effects.

After Microsoft's May 2021 update the bad request no longer reaches the read. The finders blamed a too-permissive channel: the real guest driver never sends this request, so an allow-list of expected messages would close the path.

blocks.md: **Who found it and how.** Ophir Harpaz of Guardicore Labs (now part of Akamai) and Peleg Hadar of SafeBreach Labs found it with **hAFL1**, their fuzzer for Hyper-V, and presented it at Black Hat USA 2021. Their write-up describes RNDIS set messages (a Microsoft message format for network devices) over VMBus carrying an `OID_SWITCH_NIC_REQUEST`, which wraps an inner request; "vmswitch never validates the value of OidRequest", so it could dereference a guest-chosen pointer. They found that the vulnerable code first appeared in a vmswitch build from August 2019, so it was in production for about a year and a half. Two lessons for defenders: device-side validation again (lesson 6), and a design point the finders made: netvsc, the legitimate guest driver, never sends this OID, yet vmswitch accepted it from a guest, which they called a too-permissive channel. An allow-list of expected message types would have closed it.

**Reading an advisory: what crosses a boundary?** CVSS (the Common Vulnerability Scoring System) version 3.1 has a **Scope** metric: "whenever the impact of a vulnerability breaches a security/trust boundary and impacts components outside the security scope in which vulnerable component resides, a Scope change occurs". For hypervisors, `S:C` (scope changed) is the quickest flag for "guest reaches host".

Compare **CVE-2025-21333**, exploited in the wild and added to KEV on 14 January 2025, titled "Windows Hyper-V NT Kernel Integration VSP Elevation of Privilege". It sounds like an escape, but MSRC's FAQ says the component serves "container-type VMs, such as Windows Sandbox and Microsoft Defender Application Guard", "is not in a traditional Hyper-V VM environment", and the result is SYSTEM on the local machine. Its vector is local with scope unchanged. Urgent, because it is exploited, but a local privilege escalation, not a VM escape. Also read PR with the text: Broadcom scores CVE-2025-22224 PR:N although the attacker needs admin rights inside the guest.

blocks.caption: Triage three advisories by their published CVSS 3.1 vectors.

blocks.code:
$ python3 l11_cvss.py
CVE-2021-28476 Hyper-V vmswitch    AV=network  PR=L  scope CHANGED: crosses a boundary
CVE-2025-21333 Hyper-V NT VSP      AV=local    PR=L  scope unchanged
CVE-2025-22224 ESXi VMCI           AV=local    PR=N  scope CHANGED: crosses a boundary

blocks.md: Do not triage by product name. "Hyper-V" in a title does not mean guest-to-host, and a 9.9 with "Exploitation Less Likely" (CVE-2021-28476) may be less urgent today than a 7.8 that is already exploited (CVE-2025-21333). Read the impact text, the scope, and the KEV status together.

blocks.question: CVE-2021-28476 usually led to a host crash rather than code execution. Why was it still scored 9.9?
options: A guest could crash the host (every tenant down) over a network-reachable path with low privileges, scope changed, and reads of device registers could have further side effects
Because Microsoft scores all Hyper-V bugs as critical
Because it was exploited in the wild
Because the bug was in a user-mode process
blocks.explain: The vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. The scope change (guest to host) and the high impact ratings drive the score. MSRC listed it as not exploited, 'Exploitation Less Likely'.

blocks.question: Which signal in an advisory most directly says 'a guest can affect the host or other guests'?
options: The word 'Hyper-V' or 'ESXi' in the title
A base score above 9.0
CVSS Scope: Changed (S:C), backed by impact text describing the host
Attack Vector: Network
blocks.explain: Scope captures crossing a security authority's boundary. Titles mislead (CVE-2025-21333), scores mix many factors, and AV:N describes the path, not the boundary.

lessons.title: The management plane: ESXiArgs, SLP and locking down hosts

blocks.md:
Plain idea: you do not need a VM escape if you can log in to the hypervisor, or exploit a service on its management interface. The **management plane** is everything used to administer the host: web consoles, SSH, APIs, discovery services, and managers such as vCenter. Whoever controls it controls every VM on the host.

**ESXiArgs, February 2023.** On 3 February 2023 France's [CERT-FR](https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/alerte/CERTFR-2023-ALE-015/) warned of campaigns encrypting VMware ESXi hosts. Attackers seemed to target **SLP** (Service Location Protocol, a network discovery service), where VMware had fixed several bugs, notably CVE-2020-3992 and CVE-2021-21974. Exploit code had been public since at least May 2021, and the hosts hit appeared to be ESXi 6.x before 6.7. CVE-2021-21974 was an OpenSLP heap overflow reachable by "a malicious actor residing within the same network segment as ESXi who has access to port 427", fixed in [VMSA-2021-0002](https://www.vmware.com/security/advisories/VMSA-2021-0002.html) on 23 February 2021: almost two years before the campaign.

blocks.title: From patch to mass exploitation (months after the February 2021 fix)

scenes.caption: February 2021: VMSA-2021-0002 fixes the OpenSLP heap overflow CVE-2021-21974. Every host patched from here on is safe from it.
From about May 2021, according to CERT-FR, exploit code for the SLP bugs is public. Unpatched, internet-facing hosts are now exposed to anyone.
February 2023, month 24: the ESXiArgs campaign encrypts thousands of unpatched, exposed hosts. CISA and the FBI later count over 3,800.
Days later: CERT-FR (3 Feb), the CISA and FBI advisory with a recovery script (8 Feb), and a new attack wave the same day that encrypted more of each file.

blocks.md:
**What the ransomware did, and why recovery was sometimes possible.** The joint CISA and FBI advisory AA23-039A (8 February 2023) says ESXiArgs "encrypts configuration files associated with the VMs; it does not encrypt flat files", so victims could sometimes rebuild the small descriptor files from the untouched `-flat.vmdk` disk data. CISA published a recovery script on GitHub and warned to review it before use. CERT-FR's update of 10 February reported that a new wave starting 8 February changed the encryption to cover more of large files, making restoration much harder or impossible. CISA's recommendations were blunt: update ESXi, "disabling the Service Location Protocol (SLP) service", and "Ensure the ESXi hypervisor is not exposed to the public internet."

The lesson is not the specific CVE: CISA itself only said actors "may be exploiting known vulnerabilities". It is that an unpatched, internet-reachable management service on a hypervisor turns one bug into thousands of encrypted hosts.

**Locking a host down.** Broadcom's KB on **lockdown mode** describes two levels. In *normal* mode the host is managed through vCenter, and the DCUI (Direct Console User Interface, the host's local console) stays available only to listed **exception users** with admin rights and to users named in the `DCUI.Access` option, for emergencies. In *strict* mode the DCUI service is stopped too; if vCenter is lost, "the ESXi host becomes unavailable unless the ESXi Shell and SSH services are enabled and Exception Users are defined". The KB warns that "Adding ESXi administrators to this list defeats the purpose of lockdown mode."

**execInstalledOnly** is ESXi's answer to dropped binaries: a host runs only programs from installed packages (VIBs, vSphere Installation Bundles). Broadcom's KB 344815 gives the exact log lines when ESXi 8.0 blocks or merely warns about a non-installed binary, and when the protection is switched off. Elastic, maker of the Elasticsearch-based Elastic Security platform, ships a prebuilt detection rule for the switch-off. The scanner below uses those formats.

blocks.caption: Scan forwarded ESXi vobd.log lines (synthetic, in the formats from Broadcom KB 344815) and a host's settings for the signs that preceded host-wide encryption.

blocks.code:
$ python3 l12_esxi.py
HIGH  protection switched off | 03:14:07 ExecInstalledOnly has been disabled.
MED   unknown binary blocked | 03:15:41 Execution of non-installed file prevented: /tmp/enc
HIGH  unknown binary allowed | 03:16:02 Execution of non-installed file: /tmp/enc
FIX   SLP running: disable it (ESXiArgs)
FIX   lockdown mode off
FIX   SSH enabled outside maintenance

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevent: patch ESXi and vCenter on vendor and KEV timelines; disable SLP and SSH; never expose management interfaces to the internet; put them on a separate management network; use lockdown mode and execInstalledOnly; keep hosts joined to Active Directory (AD, Microsoft's directory service) out of reach of ordinary domain accounts (CVE-2024-37085, which let anyone able to re-create a configured AD admin group take over the host, is in KEV as used by ransomware). Detect: forward ESXi logs off the host (an attacker with root on it can edit local logs), and alert on SSH enablement, execInstalledOnly changes, new local accounts and mass VM power-offs. Respond: isolate the host, preserve logs, rebuild from known-good media and restore VMs from backups the attacker could not reach.

blocks.question: CVE-2021-21974 was patched in February 2021. Why were thousands of hosts still encrypted in February 2023?
options: Many hosts stayed unpatched (including end-of-life 6.x versions) with SLP reachable from the internet, and exploit code had been public since 2021
The patch did not work
ESXiArgs used a new zero-day only
Lockdown mode was on by default and blocked patching
blocks.explain: CERT-FR and CISA both point at unpatched, out-of-date or end-of-life hosts with exposed services. The fix existed for two years; exposure plus delay did the rest.

blocks.question: An admin enables strict lockdown mode on every host, with no exception users and SSH disabled, and vCenter then fails. What happens, per Broadcom's KB?
options: Hosts fall back to normal lockdown automatically
The DCUI still allows root to log in
Nothing; strict mode only affects the web client
The hosts become unmanageable until vCenter is restored; if it cannot be, reinstalling ESXi may be required
blocks.explain: Strict mode stops the DCUI. Without exception users and SSH or Shell enabled, losing vCenter leaves no way in, and the KB says a reinstall may be required. Plan break-glass access before turning it on.

lessons.title: Side channels across VMs: what the hypervisor must flush and isolate

blocks.md:
Plain idea: two VMs that never share a byte of memory still share a CPU core's caches, internal buffers and branch predictors. These are transient-execution bugs: the CPU runs instructions speculatively, discards the results, but leaves traces in caches and buffers. **Spectre** abuses mistrained branch prediction; **L1TF** (L1 Terminal Fault, also called Foreshadow) reads the L1 data cache through a page table entry marked not present; **MDS** (Microarchitectural Data Sampling) leaks data from CPU internal buffers. The Side channels and hardware security course covers the attacks in depth. This lesson is about the hypervisor's side of the bargain: what it must clean up at each **VM entry** and **VM exit**, and what it must keep apart in time and space.

Tiny example: VM A and the host kernel run on the two **hyperthreads** (SMT siblings: two logical CPUs sharing one physical core) of core 0. Flushing core 0's L1 data cache when VM A enters does nothing about data the host brings into that same cache a microsecond later from the sibling thread.

**L1TF in a VM.** Linux's L1TF documentation explains why VMs are special: a malicious guest controls its own page table entries directly, so it can aim the flaw at host physical memory, but "only ... data which is present in L1D". Mitigations, as the kernel documents them:

- **L1D flush on VMENTER**: "the hypervisor flushes the L1D before entering the guest". Observed cost: "performance degradation in the range of 1% to 50%", depending on how often the guest exits. The default is *conditional* mode, which skips the flush after exits that ran only audited code.
- But "L1D flush does not prevent the SMT problem because the sibling thread will also bring back its data into the L1D".
- So: confine a guest's vCPUs to dedicated physical cores, steer interrupts away from them, or disable SMT.

**MDS.** CPU buffers are cleared before entering a guest; on L1TF-affected CPUs the L1D flush does it. The kernel's verdict for untrusted guests: "If the MDS mitigation is enabled and SMT is disabled, guest to host and guest to guest attacks are prevented."

scenes.caption: VM A runs on thread 0 while the host kernel handles interrupts on thread 1. Both fill the same L1 data cache, so host data sits where VM A can probe it.
VM A exits; the host handles it on thread 0 and flushes L1D just before re-entering VM A. Thread 0's own host data is gone.
But the sibling keeps running host code and refills L1D within microseconds. The flush protected one moment, not the core: the SMT problem the kernel docs describe.

Core scheduling: only one trusted group shares a core, so thread 1 runs VM A's other vCPU or idles. Better, not complete: host exit code (4 to 6 us) still shares the core with vCPU 2, so the kernel says it mitigates some, not all, cross-thread attacks.

blocks.md: **Branch predictors at VM exit.** Linux's Spectre documentation lists what KVM hosts do by default: against a guest poisoning predictions used by the host kernel, "retpoline or Enhanced IBRS" (retpoline, short for return trampoline, traps speculation of indirect branches; IBRS, indirect branch restricted speculation, is the CPU feature that does the same in hardware), plus flushing "the return stack buffer on every VM exit" (the predictor for return addresses); against guest-to-guest attacks on one hardware thread, the branch target buffer "is sanitized by flushing before switching to a new guest on a CPU" (that flush is **IBPB**, indirect branch prediction barrier).

**VMSCAPE (2025).** Researchers at ETH Zurich's COMSEC group showed that this still left a gap: the guest could steer predictions used by the *user-space* VMM. The CVE is CVE-2025-40300. Linux's documentation explains the gap: the existing Spectre v2 mitigations "are applied at context switch time, while the userspace VMM can run after a VM-exit without a context switch". Their demonstration leaked secrets from QEMU on AMD Zen 4 and Zen 5. The fix is an IBPB "before the first exit to userspace after VM-exit", reported in `/sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/vmscape` as "Mitigation: IBPB before exit to userspace". Lesson 5's sandboxed QEMU process turned out to need protecting *from* the guest's influence on the CPU too.

**Choosing the policy.** Linux groups these mitigations into **attack vector controls**. Guest-to-host and guest-to-guest mitigations "are enabled by default if KVM support is present"; cross-thread mitigations are only partly enabled by default, because many need SMT off. `mitigations=auto,nosmt` turns on everything including SMT disabling. **Core scheduling** (`CONFIG_SCHED_CORE`) lets you keep SMT on while making sure "tasks that are not in the same group never run simultaneously on a core"; the kernel notes it "can mitigate some (not all) cross-HT attacks".

Firecracker's production guide adds three host settings for multi-tenant hosts: disable SMT, disable **KSM** (kernel samepage merging, which deduplicates identical pages and so opens side channels that reveal which pages another process accesses), and use ECC (error-correcting code) memory with mitigations for Rowhammer, a DRAM flaw that "can lead to unauthorized cross-process memory changes". It also states the limit plainly: "Firecracker is not able to mitigate host's hardware vulnerabilities."

blocks.caption: Review a KVM host's vulnerability files (synthetic: each line uses the exact format of the kernel's arch/x86/kernel/cpu/bugs.c, but the lines are mixed from different CPU generations, so no single real CPU prints all four).

blocks.code:
$ python3 l13_vulns.py
REVIEW  l1tf: guest and host can share a core via SMT
REVIEW  mds: guest and host can share a core via SMT
ok      spectre_v2: Mitigation: Enhanced / Automatic IBRS
UNKNOWN vmscape: no file, kernel predates this check: update it
REVIEW  SMT active with untrusted guests: nosmt or core scheduling

blocks.md: Note the `UNKNOWN` line: on a kernel too old to know about VMSCAPE, the file simply does not exist. A missing file is not "not affected"; it means the kernel cannot tell you. Fleet inventories should flag missing files for issues newer than the kernel.

"We flush on VM entry, so we are safe" is the classic half-fix. A flush protects a moment on one hardware thread. If a sibling thread runs another tenant or the host, the data comes back. Cross-tenant hosts need flushes AND isolation in space: no SMT sharing across trust boundaries.

blocks.question: A KVM host flushes L1D unconditionally on every VM entry, keeps SMT on, and lets any vCPU run on any thread. Is VM A's L1TF exposure to host data closed?
options: Yes, the flush removes all host data before VM A runs
No: a sibling hyperthread running host code (or another VM) refills the shared L1D while VM A runs
Yes, because EPT blocks L1TF
No, because the flush is only conditional
blocks.explain: The kernel's L1TF document: 'L1D flush does not prevent the SMT problem because the sibling thread will also bring back its data into the L1D'. Unconditional mode does not change that; dedicated cores, core scheduling or nosmt do.

blocks.question: Why did VMSCAPE need a new mitigation even though IBPB was already used when switching between guests and processes?
options: Because AMD CPUs do not support IBPB
Because the user-space VMM runs right after a VM exit without a context switch, so no existing barrier ran between the guest's training and QEMU's use of the predictor
Because QEMU runs as root
Because the guest could disable IBPB
blocks.explain: Linux's VMSCAPE page says exactly this: mitigations applied at context switch time miss the guest-to-VMM transition. The fix issues IBPB before the first return to user space after a VM exit.

lessons.title: Confidential VMs: SEV-SNP, TDX and Arm CCA stop trusting the host

blocks.md:
Plain idea: so far the host was trusted and the guest was not. Flip it. A hospital wants to run a VM in a public cloud without trusting the cloud's administrators, hypervisor or firmware updates. **Confidential computing** aims to protect data *in use*; Linux's threat-model document for x86 describes the confidential VM's new adversary as "a potentially misbehaving host (which can also include some part of a traditional VMM or all of it)", placed outside the guest's TCB "due to its large SW attack surface".

The security objectives, per that document: "Preserve the confidentiality and integrity of CoCo guest's private memory and registers" and "Prevent privileged escalation from a host into a CoCo guest Linux kernel". Explicitly *not* covered: the host can still deny service at any time, by withholding CPU time, memory or network.

**AMD SEV, in three generations** (from AMD's developer page):

- **SEV** (Secure Encrypted Virtualization, first in EPYC 7001): each VM's memory is encrypted with its own key, held by the **AMD Secure Processor** and selected by the VM's ASID (address space identifier). The host reads only ciphertext.
- **SEV-ES** (Encrypted State, EPYC 7002): "encrypts all CPU register contents when a VM stops running", so a VM exit no longer hands the hypervisor the guest's registers.
- **SEV-SNP** (Secure Nested Paging, EPYC 7003): adds "strong memory integrity protection to help prevent malicious hypervisor-based attacks like data replay, memory re-mapping".

The SNP mechanism is the **RMP** (reverse map table), one entry per physical page, which per AMD's ABI specification "ensures that a page cannot be mapped into multiple guests at once, and it cannot be mapped multiple times into a single guest at once". The guest marks pages it expects to be protected with the `PVALIDATE` instruction.

Encryption alone (plain SEV) left a gap: a hypervisor that cannot read memory can still swap, replay or remap encrypted pages. SNP's RMP closes that gap.

blocks.title: Who is trusted: classic VM versus confidential VM

nodes.label:
trusted firmware:
AMD-SP / TDX module / RMM

scenes.caption: Classic VM: the guest trusts the whole host stack. Whoever runs the hypervisor can read and change guest memory and registers.
Confidential VM: a small trusted component (AMD Secure Processor firmware, Intel's TDX module, or Arm's RMM) plus CPU encryption protect guest memory and registers.
The host still schedules, allocates and destroys the VM, but only by asking the trusted firmware, which enforces the rules. Denial of service stays possible.
I/O still goes through pages the guest deliberately shares with the host. Everything arriving there is untrusted input to the guest kernel.

blocks.md: **Intel TDX** (Trust Domain Extensions; a confidential VM is a **TD**, trust domain). Linux's TDX documentation: TDX "introduces a new CPU mode called Secure Arbitration Mode (SEAM)" with a protected memory range, where "a CPU-attested software module called 'the TDX module'" manages TDs. Memory is encrypted with **MKTME** (multi-key total memory encryption), and TDX-private key IDs "are only accessible within the SEAM mode". Guest memory is either *private*, "protected against access from the hypervisor", or *shared* with it, chosen per page by a page-table bit; instructions the TDX module will not handle raise a **#VE** (virtualization exception) inside the guest, which may then ask the hypervisor through a hypercall.

**Arm CCA** (Confidential Compute Architecture). Arm systems with RME (Realm Management Extension) have four "worlds": Normal, Secure, Root and **Realm**. Per Linux's documentation, the **RMM** (Realm Management Monitor) in the Realm world "acts a bit like a hypervisor", but "much of the control is handled by a hypervisor running in the Normal World", which asks the RMM to act. The guest's address space is split: the lower half is protected, the upper half shared with the host. Arm's own page adds that the RMM "does not make policy decisions, such as which Realm to run or what memory to allocate".

blocks.code:
# Toy reverse map table: one entry per host physical page (simplified;
# the real RMP also holds page size, VMPL permissions and more).
rmp = {}   # host page: {"owner", "gpa", "validated"}

def assign(page, guest, gpa):
    e = rmp.get(page)
    if e and e["owner"] != "hypervisor":
        return f"refused: page {page:#x} already belongs to {e['owner']}"
    rmp[page] = {"owner": guest, "gpa": gpa, "validated": False}
    return f"page {page:#x} assigned to {guest} at gPA {gpa:#x}"

def pvalidate(page, guest, gpa):         # run by the guest itself
    e = rmp[page]
    if e["owner"] == guest and e["gpa"] == gpa:
        e["validated"] = True
        return "validated"
    return "validation failed: not the page the guest expected"

def access(page, who, gpa=None):
    e = rmp.get(page, {"owner": "hypervisor"})
    if e["owner"] == who and (who == "hypervisor" or
                              (e["gpa"] == gpa and e["validated"])):
        return f"{who} access to {page:#x} ok"
    return f"{who} access to {page:#x}: RMP check fails"

print(assign(0x50, "vmA", 0x1000)); print(pvalidate(0x50, "vmA", 0x1000))
print(access(0x50, "vmA", 0x1000))
print(access(0x50, "hypervisor"))          # host tries to write guest memory
print(assign(0x50, "vmB", 0x1000))         # host tries to map it twice
print(access(0x50, "vmA", 0x2000))         # host remapped it at another gPA
blocks.caption: A toy reverse map table: the host can still assign pages, but cannot write a guest-owned page (a read returns only ciphertext), map it twice, or quietly move it to a different guest address.

blocks.code:
$ python3 l14_rmp.py
page 0x50 assigned to vmA at gPA 0x1000
validated
vmA access to 0x50 ok
hypervisor access to 0x50: RMP check fails
refused: page 0x50 already belongs to vmA
vmA access to 0x50: RMP check fails

blocks.md: **The guest becomes the defender.** With the host untrusted, every interface the guest kernel shares with it becomes attack surface: port I/O, MMIO, DMA, PCI configuration space, hypercalls, shared pages and injected interrupts, plus side channels, which Linux's threat model lists explicitly. Its threat matrix includes "Malformed runtime input" and "Malicious runtime input", such as "a malicious time" or tampered entropy. Practical consequences: encrypt network and disk traffic inside the guest (the host still carries it), harden guest drivers against hostile devices, and verify the boot chain by attestation before trusting the VM with anything. Devices are the next frontier: AMD's SEV-TIO and the PCI-SIG's TDISP protocol aim to bring PCIe devices inside the trust boundary.

A confidential VM moves trust from the host's software to the CPU vendor's hardware and firmware. It protects memory and registers from a curious or compromised host, not availability, not the guest's own bugs, and not data the guest sends through shared pages unencrypted.

blocks.question: Plain SEV encrypts each VM's memory. What attack did SEV-SNP's reverse map table add protection against?
options: Reading guest memory in plaintext
Denial of service by the host
Side channels through shared caches
The hypervisor remapping or replaying encrypted guest pages, for example mapping one page twice
blocks.explain: Encryption hides contents but not placement. A hypervisor that controls the nested page tables could swap or replay ciphertext pages. The RMP enforces one owner and one guest address per page; denial of service remains out of scope.

blocks.question: In TDX and Arm CCA alike, guest memory is split into protected and shared parts. Which data should a well-built confidential guest put in shared memory?
options: Only data meant for the host, such as I/O buffers, ideally already encrypted by the guest
Kernel stacks and page tables
Disk encryption keys, so the host can back them up
Nothing; shared memory is unused
blocks.explain: Linux's TDX docs: 'Shared mappings must never be used for sensitive memory content'. Shared pages exist for I/O and communication with the host, which controls them completely.

lessons.title: Attestation: proving what is running before you send it secrets

blocks.md:
Plain idea: encryption is useless if the cloud can start a *different* VM, one with a backdoor, and you send your database key to it. **Attestation** lets the trusted hardware sign a statement: "this VM was launched with exactly these contents, under this policy, on genuine hardware at this firmware level". A **relying party** (verifier) checks the statement and only then releases secrets. To stop replays, the verifier first sends a fresh **nonce** (a number used once), and the signed statement must contain it, so an old statement cannot pass as new. In a confidential VM, the CPU vendor's firmware is the signer.

On AMD SEV-SNP, the guest asks the AMD Secure Processor for an **attestation report** (Linux exposes this as the `SNP_GET_REPORT` ioctl on `/dev/sev-guest`). The guest supplies 64 bytes of **REPORT_DATA**, commonly a hash of the verifier's nonce and a public key the VM just generated, so the report is bound both to this request and to the channel the secret will travel over.

blocks.title: Releasing a disk key to an SEV-SNP VM

scenes.caption: The VM boots from an image whose launch measurement the owner computed in advance. It needs a disk key it does not have.
The verifier answers with a fresh nonce, so an old report cannot be replayed.
The VM asks the firmware for a report with REPORT_DATA = hash(nonce, its new public key). The host relays the request but cannot read or alter it.
The VM sends the report and certificate chain. The verifier checks signature, measurement, policy, TCB and the nonce binding.
Only if every check passes is the key released, encrypted to the public key named in REPORT_DATA, which only that VM holds.

blocks.md:
**What is in the report.** AMD's SNP firmware ABI specification (publication 56860, table 23) fixes the layout: 1184 bytes (0x4A0), with the signature over bytes 0x0 to 0x29F. Fields a verifier must check:

- **MEASUREMENT** (0x90, 48 bytes): "The measurement calculated at launch", a hash of the initial guest memory. Compare with the value you computed from your own image.
- **REPORT_DATA** (0x50, 64 bytes): your nonce binding.
- **POLICY** (0x08): the guest policy fixed at launch. Bit 19 is DEBUG; if set, the firmware's debug commands can decrypt the guest's memory for the host. Bit 16 allows SMT.
- **REPORTED_TCB** (0x180): security version numbers of the firmware components and microcode; reject values below your minimum.
- **PLATFORM_INFO** (0x40): platform facts such as SMT enabled (bit 0) and ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE (bit 5, see BadRAM below).
- **SIGNATURE** (0x2A0): ECDSA (elliptic-curve signature) P-384, by the **VCEK** (versioned chip endorsement key, from chip secrets and a TCB version) or a cloud provider's **VLEK** (versioned loaded endorsement key), chained to AMD's root.

blocks.code:
# Build a SYNTHETIC SEV-SNP attestation report using the byte offsets of
# Table 23 in AMD's SNP firmware ABI spec (56860). Not a real report.
import hashlib, struct
def tcb(boot, tee, snp, ucode):          # Milan/Genoa TCB_VERSION layout
    return boot | tee << 8 | snp << 48 | ucode << 56

def make_report(nonce, measurement, debug=False, tcb_v=tcb(3, 0, 8, 115),
                alias_checked=True):
    r = bytearray(0x4A0)                 # 1184 bytes; signature at 0x2A0
    policy = (1 << 17) | (1 << 16) | (debug << 19)   # bit 17 must be one
    struct.pack_into("<IIQ", r, 0x00, 5, 1, policy)  # VERSION, GUEST_SVN, POLICY
    struct.pack_into("<II", r, 0x30, 0, 1)           # VMPL 0, ECDSA P-384
    struct.pack_into("<QQ", r, 0x38, tcb_v, 1 | alias_checked << 5)  # CURRENT_TCB, PLATFORM_INFO
    r[0x50:0x90] = hashlib.sha512(nonce).digest()    # REPORT_DATA (64 bytes)
    r[0x90:0xC0] = measurement                       # MEASUREMENT (48 bytes)
    struct.pack_into("<Q", r, 0x180, tcb_v)          # REPORTED_TCB
    return bytes(r)
blocks.caption: Build a synthetic report with the spec's offsets (this is test data for the verifier, not a real report).

A verifier for the fields above. Signature checking is described, not implemented: a real verifier must validate the ECDSA signature and the AMD certificate chain first, using a maintained library. For brevity REPORT_DATA here hashes only the nonce; a real one also binds the VM's new public key.

blocks.code:
$ python3 snp_verify.py
good 1184 bytes
   all checks passed: release the secret
bad 1184 bytes
   REPORT_DATA does not bind our nonce (replay?)
   POLICY.DEBUG=1: host may read guest memory
   TCB snp=7 below 8
   ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE=0: no BadRAM mitigation proof

blocks.md:
**Case: BadRAM (2024).** Researchers from KU Leuven, the University of Lübeck and the University of Birmingham (IEEE S&P 2025) showed that a memory module's **SPD** (serial presence detect) chip, which tells the CPU the module's size at boot, can be reprogrammed to lie. The CPU then sees two addresses for the same DRAM cell, an **alias**, and SNP's protections, which assume one address per cell, fail: the researchers replayed memory and faked attestation. AMD-SB-3015 (CVE-2024-21944, CVSS 5.3) blames improper validation of SPD data.

The fix added a boot-time alias check, *reported in the attestation report*: PLATFORM_INFO bit 5, ALIAS_CHECK_COMPLETE, "alias detection has completed since the last system reset and there are no aliasing addresses." The verifier above demands it. But it proves only a boot-time check: in 2025 Battering RAM (KU Leuven and Birmingham) used a cheap memory-bus interposer that starts aliasing after boot and broke SNP attestation on patched systems. Physical access stays outside what SNP can stop.

**Intel TDX and Arm CCA, briefly.** In TDX, the TDX module records the build-time measurement in **MRTD** (the TD's build-time measurement register) and runtime measurements (kernel, command line, initrd, ACPI tables) in **RTMRs** (runtime measurement registers). A TD gets a **TDREPORT** with 64 bytes of REPORTDATA; because the TDREPORT's MAC "can only be verified on the local platform", an Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) **Quoting Enclave** converts it into a remotely verifiable **Quote**. In Arm CCA, a Realm requests attestation from the RMM through the Realm Services Interface. The verifier logic is the same everywhere: signature chain, measurement, policy, firmware versions, freshness.

The most common attestation bug is not cryptographic: a verifier that checks the signature but not the nonce (replay), not the measurement (any VM passes), or not the debug policy (the host can decrypt). Check every field you depend on, and fail closed.

blocks.question: A verifier checks the report's signature chain and the MEASUREMENT, but never looks at REPORT_DATA. What can a malicious host do?
options: Nothing; the signature covers everything
Change the measurement without breaking the signature
Replay a genuine report from an earlier boot of the right image to a fake VM, and receive the secret
Disable SMT
blocks.explain: REPORT_DATA binds the report to this request and to the key the secret will be sealed to. Without that check, any old valid report proves nothing about the VM asking now.

blocks.question: Why does a SEV-SNP verifier reject reports with POLICY bit 19 set, even when the measurement is correct?
options: Bit 19 means SMT is enabled
Bit 19 marks an old report format
Bit 19 means the VCEK was not used
Bit 19 is DEBUG: the firmware's debug commands could then decrypt guest memory for the host, undoing the confidentiality the verifier is relying on
blocks.explain: The ABI spec defines bit 19 as DEBUG, and the firmware's SNP_DBG_DECRYPT command only works when the guest's policy allows debugging. A debuggable confidential VM is not confidential.

lessons.title: A defender's playbook for virtualization, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Plain idea: pull the course together into one checklist per layer, with the signal each layer produces. Everything below was introduced in an earlier lesson.

**Design and build:**

- Expose the fewest devices: virtio or a microVM machine type instead of legacy emulation (lessons 5 to 8). On QEMU, consider `-compat insecure-input=reject`.
- Put device models in per-VM, unprivileged sandboxes: QEMU as a non-root user with SELinux or AppArmor and `--sandbox`; Firecracker only through its jailer; Xen stub domains or PVH (lesson 9).
- One tenant per VMM process, and no SMT sharing between tenants: core scheduling or `nosmt`; KSM off on multi-tenant hosts (lesson 13).
- Use the IOMMU for any device assignment, and assign whole IOMMU groups (lesson 4).
- For workloads that must not trust the host: confidential VMs, with a verifier that checks every report field (lessons 14 and 15).

**Operate:**

- Patch the hypervisor, the VMM, the host kernel and CPU microcode together; many fixes need all of them. Track vendor advisories (VMSA, XSA, MSRC) and CISA's KEV catalogue; "exploited in the wild" moves a fix to the front of the queue (lessons 10 and 11).
- Treat the management plane as tier zero: separate network, no internet exposure, SLP and SSH off, lockdown mode, execInstalledOnly, logs forwarded off the host (lesson 12).
- Inventory `/sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities` across the fleet and flag missing files (lesson 13).

**Respond:** if a VM escape is suspected, treat the *host* as compromised, not just the VM: every VM on it, the host's credentials and anything the host could reach. Preserve host logs and memory where possible, migrate clean workloads to patched hosts, rebuild the host from known-good media, and rotate secrets that passed through any VM on it.

scenes.caption: Device models: a crash, a seccomp kill or an SELinux denial in a VMM process can be a failed escape attempt. Alert on them per VM.
Hypervisor and kernel: exposure comes from advisories and KEV; live signals are IOMMU faults from assigned devices and unexplained host crashes.
CPU: side channels leave no logs, so the signal is exposure, collected fleet-wide from sysfs and microcode versions.
Management plane: ransomware crews log in rather than escape. Configuration changes and mass VM power-offs are often the first visible step.

blocks.md: The boundary between VMs is code you can shrink, sandbox, patch and watch: device models, exit handlers, management services. Hardware gives you the tools (VMX/SVM, EPT/NPT, IOMMU, SNP/TDX/CCA), but every real escape in this course went through software someone could have removed, confined or updated sooner.

**Practise legally.** Every script in this course is standard-library Python and changes nothing on your machine; extend them. Give ToyFIFO a DMA command and fuzz it with an invariant that DMA stays inside guest RAM. Add a race to the descriptor checker. Make the attestation verifier reject reports whose TCB is lower than the one in your last accepted report (rollback). On a Linux machine you own, *read* (do not change) `/sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/` and `dmesg | grep -i -e DMAR -e AMD-Vi` to see your own CPU's mitigations and IOMMU state.

For broader systems practice, [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/) teaches low-level exploitation and defence down to the kernel, and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (the new home of picoCTF) runs capture-the-flag practice. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test; a cloud provider's hypervisor is never yours to test outside its published bug bounty rules.

blocks.question: An alert shows that a customer VM's QEMU process was killed by seccomp after attempting an unexpected system call. What is the best first response?
options: Ignore it; seccomp worked
Disable seccomp for that VM so it stops crashing
Reboot the host immediately and delete the logs
Treat it as a possible escape attempt: preserve the event and the VM's state, check the host for other signs, and review whether the guest's activity triggered a device-model bug
blocks.explain: A device model making a system call outside its allow-list is what a successful device bug followed by a failed sandbox step looks like. Containment worked, but the bug still exists; investigate and patch.

blocks.question: Which single change most reduces the impact of the next VENOM-style device bug on a KVM host?
options: Raising the guest's RAM
Turning off EPT
Running QEMU unprivileged and confined (SELinux/AppArmor, seccomp), with only the devices each VM needs
Using larger pages for guest memory
blocks.explain: VENOM's impact was 'the privileges of the host's QEMU process'. Fewer devices shrink the chance of a bug; a confined, unprivileged QEMU shrinks what a bug gives. EPT and page size do not touch device emulation.
